questions.question: What are the four pillars of object-oriented programming? Explain each briefly.
questions.ideal_answer: The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that operate on it inside a class and hides internal state behind access modifiers. Abstraction exposes only essential behaviour through interfaces or abstract classes and hides implementation details. Inheritance lets a child class reuse and extend the properties and methods of a parent class. Polymorphism lets the same method call behave differently depending on the object, through method overriding at runtime or overloading at compile time.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array and a linked list? When would you use each?
questions.ideal_answer: An array stores elements in contiguous memory, so it gives O(1) random access by index but insertion and deletion in the middle cost O(n) because elements must shift, and a static array has a fixed size. A linked list stores nodes that hold a value and a pointer to the next node, so insertion and deletion at a known position are O(1) but access by index is O(n) and it uses extra memory for pointers and has poor cache locality. Use arrays when you need fast indexed access and the size is fairly stable; use linked lists when you do frequent insertions and deletions, such as implementing queues or LRU caches.

questions.question: What is Git and what is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
questions.ideal_answer: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes to code, lets developers work on branches in parallel and keeps a full history in every clone. git merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit that preserves both histories exactly as they happened. git rebase moves or replays the commits of one branch on top of another, producing a linear history without a merge commit. Rebase gives a cleaner history but rewrites commits, so you should not rebase shared public branches; merge is safer for shared branches.

questions.question: Explain how a hash map works internally and how collisions are handled.
questions.ideal_answer: A hash map stores key-value pairs in an array of buckets. A hash function converts the key into an integer that is mapped to a bucket index, giving average O(1) insert, lookup and delete. A collision happens when two keys map to the same bucket. It is handled with separate chaining, where each bucket holds a linked list or tree of entries, or with open addressing, where the map probes other slots using linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing. When the load factor crosses a threshold the table is resized and all keys are rehashed, which keeps operations close to O(1); in the worst case operations degrade to O(n).

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread? What is a deadlock?
questions.ideal_answer: A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space, while threads are lighter units of execution inside a process that share its memory and resources. Context switching between threads is cheaper, but shared memory requires synchronisation with locks, mutexes or semaphores to avoid race conditions. A deadlock is when two or more threads wait forever for resources held by each other. It requires four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. It can be prevented by breaking one condition, for example by acquiring locks in a fixed global order or using timeouts.

questions.question: What are ACID properties in databases, and what is the purpose of an index?
questions.ideal_answer: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Atomicity means a transaction completes fully or not at all. Consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not interfere, controlled by isolation levels. Durability means committed data survives crashes. An index is a data structure, usually a B-tree or hash, that speeds up lookups and range queries on columns at the cost of extra storage and slower writes, because the index must be updated on insert, update and delete.

questions.question: How would you design a URL shortening service like bit.ly?
questions.ideal_answer: Requirements: generate a short unique code for a long URL, redirect quickly, handle very high read traffic and optionally track analytics. Generate codes with base62 encoding of an auto-increment or distributed ID generator such as Snowflake, or a hash with collision checks. Store the mapping in a key-value or NoSQL store that scales horizontally, sharded by the short code. Reads far outnumber writes, so put a cache such as Redis in front of the database and use a CDN where possible. Redirect with HTTP 301 or 302. Use load balancers and stateless application servers, add rate limiting to prevent abuse, handle expiry, and record click analytics asynchronously through a message queue.

questions.question: Explain the CAP theorem and how it influences the design of distributed databases.
questions.ideal_answer: The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency, where every read sees the latest write, and availability, where every request receives a response. Partition tolerance is not optional in real networks, so the real trade-off is CP versus AP. CP systems such as HBase or ZooKeeper reject or delay requests to stay consistent; AP systems such as Cassandra or DynamoDB keep responding and reach eventual consistency. Designers choose based on the business need, for example strong consistency for payments and eventual consistency for social feeds, and often use tunable consistency with quorum reads and writes. PACELC extends CAP by noting the latency versus consistency trade-off even without partitions.

questions.question: Explain the SOLID principles with an example of applying one of them.
questions.ideal_answer: SOLID stands for Single Responsibility, Open-Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Single responsibility means a class should have one reason to change. Open-closed means code should be open for extension but closed for modification. Liskov substitution means subclasses must be usable wherever the parent is expected without breaking behaviour. Interface segregation means clients should not depend on methods they do not use, so prefer small focused interfaces. Dependency inversion means high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. For example, a PaymentService that depends on a PaymentGateway interface instead of a concrete Stripe class can switch providers or use a mock in tests without changing its code.

questions.question: What is the difference between mean, median and mode? When is the median preferred over the mean?
questions.ideal_answer: The mean is the arithmetic average of all values, the median is the middle value when the data is sorted, and the mode is the most frequent value. The mean uses every value, so it is sensitive to outliers and skewed data. The median is robust to outliers, so it is preferred for skewed distributions such as income or house prices. The mode is useful for categorical data.

questions.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning? Give examples.
questions.ideal_answer: Supervised learning trains a model on labelled data, where every input has a known output, to predict labels for new data. Examples are classification such as spam detection and regression such as house price prediction, using algorithms like linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees and SVM. Unsupervised learning works on unlabelled data to find hidden structure, such as clustering customers with k-means, or dimensionality reduction with PCA, and anomaly detection.

questions.question: How do you handle missing values in a dataset?
questions.ideal_answer: First understand why data is missing: completely at random, at random, or not at random. Options include dropping rows or columns when little data is missing or a column is mostly empty; imputing with the mean or median for numeric data and the mode for categorical data; using model-based imputation such as KNN or iterative imputation; forward or backward fill for time series; and adding a missing-indicator flag so the model can learn from missingness. Imputation should be fitted on training data only to avoid data leakage.

questions.question: Explain precision, recall and F1-score. When would you prioritise recall over precision?
questions.ideal_answer: Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP: of the items predicted positive, how many were actually positive. Recall is TP divided by TP plus FN: of the actual positives, how many the model found. The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall and balances the two, which is useful for imbalanced datasets where accuracy is misleading. Recall is prioritised when missing a positive is costly, such as cancer screening or fraud detection, while precision is prioritised when false alarms are costly, such as spam filtering. The trade-off is controlled by the classification threshold.

questions.question: What is overfitting and how can you prevent it?
questions.ideal_answer: Overfitting is when a model learns noise and specific details of the training data, so it performs very well on training data but poorly on unseen data; it shows high variance. It can be prevented by using more training data, cross-validation to estimate generalisation, regularisation such as L1 or L2, simplifying the model or pruning trees, early stopping, dropout in neural networks, feature selection and data augmentation, and ensemble methods such as bagging.

questions.question: What is a p-value and how do you interpret it in hypothesis testing?
questions.ideal_answer: In hypothesis testing you state a null hypothesis, usually no effect, and an alternative hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of observing results at least as extreme as the data, assuming the null hypothesis is true. If the p-value is below the chosen significance level alpha, commonly 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and statistical significance does not imply practical significance, so effect size and confidence intervals should also be reported. Type I error is rejecting a true null; type II error is failing to reject a false null.

questions.question: How would you design and analyse an A/B test for a new feature?
questions.ideal_answer: Define the hypothesis and a primary metric such as conversion rate, plus guardrail metrics. Calculate the required sample size using power analysis from the baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, significance level and power, typically 80 percent. Randomly assign users to control and treatment at the user level to avoid contamination, and run for full business cycles to avoid novelty and weekday effects. Check the sample ratio for mismatch. Analyse with an appropriate test such as a two-proportion z-test or t-test, report confidence intervals, avoid peeking or use sequential testing, and correct for multiple comparisons. Finally weigh practical significance and cost before launching.

questions.question: Explain the bias-variance trade-off and how ensemble methods address it.
questions.ideal_answer: Expected prediction error decomposes into bias squared, variance and irreducible noise. High bias means the model is too simple and underfits; high variance means it is too sensitive to the training data and overfits. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance, so we look for the balance that minimises total error. Bagging methods such as random forests average many high-variance models trained on bootstrap samples, which reduces variance. Boosting methods such as gradient boosting and XGBoost add weak learners sequentially, each correcting previous errors, which mainly reduces bias.

questions.question: How do you handle a highly imbalanced classification dataset?
questions.ideal_answer: Start by choosing the right metrics: accuracy is misleading, so use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or ROC-AUC. At the data level use resampling: oversample the minority class with SMOTE or random oversampling, or undersample the majority class, applied only to training data. At the algorithm level use class weights or cost-sensitive learning, and tune the decision threshold. Ensemble methods such as balanced random forests also help, and anomaly detection can be used when the minority class is extremely rare. Use stratified splits for cross-validation.

questions.question: What is the difference between training, validation and test sets?
questions.ideal_answer: The training set is used to fit the model's parameters. The validation set is used to tune hyperparameters, choose models and apply early stopping. The test set is held out until the end and used only once to give an unbiased estimate of performance on unseen data. A typical split is 70/15/15 or 80/10/10, and cross-validation can replace a single validation set when data is limited. Data from the test set must never leak into training.

questions.question: Explain gradient descent and the role of the learning rate.
questions.ideal_answer: Gradient descent is an optimisation algorithm that minimises a loss function by repeatedly moving the parameters in the direction of the negative gradient. The learning rate controls the step size. Too large a learning rate overshoots the minimum or diverges; too small converges very slowly or gets stuck. Variants include batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent, and optimisers such as momentum and Adam adapt the updates. Learning rate schedules decay the rate during training.

questions.question: What is an activation function and why do neural networks need one?
questions.ideal_answer: An activation function is applied to a neuron's weighted sum to produce its output. Without a non-linear activation, a stack of layers collapses into a single linear transformation, so the network could only learn linear relationships. Non-linearity lets networks approximate complex functions. Common choices are ReLU, which is fast and reduces vanishing gradients, sigmoid for binary output probabilities, tanh, and softmax for multi-class output probabilities.

questions.question: What is the vanishing gradient problem and how is it addressed?
questions.ideal_answer: During backpropagation, gradients are multiplied through many layers. With activations like sigmoid or tanh whose derivatives are small, the gradients shrink exponentially, so early layers learn very slowly or stop learning. It is addressed with ReLU-family activations, careful weight initialisation such as He or Xavier initialisation, batch normalisation, residual or skip connections as in ResNet, and gated architectures such as LSTM and GRU for recurrent networks. Gradient clipping handles the opposite exploding gradient problem.

questions.question: Explain the transformer architecture and the self-attention mechanism.
questions.ideal_answer: The transformer replaces recurrence with attention, so it processes all tokens in parallel. In self-attention each token is projected into query, key and value vectors; attention weights come from the softmax of the scaled dot product of queries and keys, divided by the square root of the key dimension, and are used to take a weighted sum of values. Multi-head attention runs several attention heads in parallel to capture different relationships. Because attention has no notion of order, positional encodings are added. Each block also has a feed-forward layer, residual connections and layer normalisation. Encoder models such as BERT and decoder models such as GPT are built from these blocks.

questions.question: What is regularisation? Compare L1 and L2 regularisation.
questions.ideal_answer: Regularisation adds a penalty on model complexity to the loss function to reduce overfitting and improve generalisation. L1, used in Lasso, adds the sum of absolute values of the weights; it drives some weights exactly to zero, so it produces sparse models and performs feature selection. L2, used in Ridge and as weight decay, adds the sum of squared weights; it shrinks weights smoothly toward zero without eliminating them and handles correlated features well. Elastic Net combines both. The strength is controlled by a hyperparameter lambda tuned with validation.

questions.question: How would you deploy and monitor a machine learning model in production?
questions.ideal_answer: Package the model with its preprocessing pipeline and pin dependencies, version it in a model registry such as MLflow, and serve it through a REST or gRPC API with FastAPI, a containerised Docker service on Kubernetes, or batch inference depending on latency needs. Use CI/CD with automated tests, and roll out safely with shadow, canary or A/B deployments. Monitor system metrics such as latency, throughput and errors, and model metrics such as prediction distribution, data drift and concept drift, comparing live features against the training distribution. Collect ground-truth labels when available to track accuracy, set alerts, and retrain on a schedule or when drift is detected, with rollback to a previous version.

questions.question: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and when would you use it instead of fine-tuning?
questions.ideal_answer: RAG retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge source at query time and passes them to an LLM as context, so answers are grounded in up-to-date or private data. A typical pipeline chunks documents, creates embeddings, stores them in a vector database, retrieves the top-k similar chunks for a query, optionally re-ranks them, and builds a prompt with the retrieved context. RAG is preferred when knowledge changes often, citations are needed, hallucinations must be reduced, or data is too large or private to bake into weights. Fine-tuning is better for changing the model's style, format or task behaviour. The two can be combined.

questions.question: How can you reduce the inference latency of a large deep learning model?
questions.ideal_answer: Options include quantisation, converting weights from FP32 to FP16, INT8 or lower; pruning unimportant weights or structures; knowledge distillation into a smaller student model; exporting to optimised runtimes such as ONNX Runtime or TensorRT with operator fusion; batching requests dynamically to raise GPU utilisation; caching repeated results and, for transformers, key-value caching; using faster hardware or GPUs; and choosing efficient architectures. Each technique should be measured against its accuracy cost on a validation set.

questions.question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
questions.ideal_answer: The browser parses the URL and checks its cache. It resolves the domain name to an IP address through DNS, using browser, OS, resolver and authoritative name server caches. It opens a TCP connection to the server and, for HTTPS, performs a TLS handshake. It sends an HTTP request; the server or load balancer processes it and returns a response with a status code, headers and body. The browser parses the HTML into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM, fetches further resources such as scripts and images, executes JavaScript, builds the render tree, then performs layout and paint to display the page.

questions.question: Explain the CSS box model.
questions.ideal_answer: Every element is rendered as a rectangular box made of four layers from inside out: content, padding, border and margin. Padding is space between content and border and takes the element's background; margin is transparent space outside the border that separates elements, and vertical margins can collapse. With box-sizing content-box, the default, width and height apply only to the content, so padding and border add to the total size; with box-sizing border-box, width includes padding and border, which makes layouts easier to reason about.

questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const in JavaScript?
questions.ideal_answer: var is function-scoped, can be redeclared, and is hoisted and initialised as undefined, which can cause bugs. let and const are block-scoped and are hoisted but stay in the temporal dead zone until their declaration, so accessing them earlier throws an error. let can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope. const cannot be reassigned, although objects and arrays declared with const can still be mutated. Modern code prefers const by default and let when reassignment is needed.

questions.question: Explain the JavaScript event loop, including the call stack and microtask queue.
questions.ideal_answer: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack. Asynchronous operations such as timers, network requests and DOM events are handled by browser or Node APIs, and their callbacks are placed in queues when ready. The event loop checks whether the call stack is empty and then moves callbacks onto it. Microtasks, such as promise callbacks and queueMicrotask, run before the next macrotask, and the whole microtask queue is drained after each task. Macrotasks include setTimeout, setInterval and I/O. That is why a resolved promise's then callback runs before a setTimeout with zero delay.

questions.question: What are REST APIs? Explain the common HTTP methods and status codes.
questions.ideal_answer: REST is an architectural style where resources are identified by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods; it is stateless, uses a uniform interface and typically exchanges JSON. GET reads a resource, POST creates one, PUT replaces it, PATCH partially updates it and DELETE removes it; GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent. Status codes: 2xx success such as 200 OK and 201 Created, 3xx redirects, 4xx client errors such as 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden and 404 Not Found, and 5xx server errors such as 500 Internal Server Error.

questions.question: What are XSS and CSRF attacks and how do you prevent them?
questions.ideal_answer: Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects malicious scripts into pages viewed by other users, for example through unsanitised input, letting attackers steal cookies or act as the user. Prevent it by escaping or encoding output, sanitising HTML input, using frameworks that auto-escape, setting a Content Security Policy and marking session cookies HttpOnly. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted authenticated request to another site. Prevent it with anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, checking Origin or Referer headers, and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions.

questions.question: How would you improve the performance of a slow-loading web application?
questions.ideal_answer: First measure with Lighthouse, Core Web Vitals such as LCP, INP and CLS, and the browser performance and network panels to find bottlenecks. On the frontend reduce bundle size with code splitting, tree shaking, minification and lazy loading; compress and resize images using modern formats such as WebP or AVIF; defer non-critical JavaScript; and avoid layout thrashing and unnecessary re-renders. On the network side use a CDN, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, Gzip or Brotli compression and caching headers. On the backend optimise slow database queries with indexes, add caching layers such as Redis, and paginate large responses. Server-side rendering or static generation can improve first paint.

questions.question: Compare session-based authentication with JWT-based authentication.
questions.ideal_answer: In session-based authentication the server creates a session after login, stores it in memory, a database or Redis, and sends the client a session ID cookie; it is easy to revoke but the server must keep state, which needs shared storage when scaling horizontally. A JWT is a signed, self-contained token holding claims such as user ID and expiry; the server verifies the signature without a lookup, so it is stateless and works well across services and APIs. JWTs are hard to revoke before expiry, so use short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens and a deny list if needed, and store them carefully, preferably in HttpOnly secure cookies rather than localStorage to limit XSS exposure.

questions.question: Explain the virtual DOM and how React's reconciliation works.
questions.ideal_answer: The virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory representation of the UI. When state or props change, React re-renders components into a new virtual tree and diffs it against the previous one, a process called reconciliation, then applies the minimum set of changes to the real DOM, which is expensive to update. The diffing algorithm is heuristic and O(n): elements of different types are replaced entirely, and keys help React match list items between renders, so stable unique keys are important. React Fiber splits rendering work into units so it can be paused and prioritised, and updates are batched.

questions.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN in SQL?
questions.ideal_answer: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have matching values in both tables. A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus the matching rows from the right table, filling NULLs where there is no match. A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image. A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, matching where possible and filling NULLs on whichever side has no match.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING clauses?
questions.ideal_answer: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and aggregation happen, so it cannot use aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation, so it can use aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM or AVG. For example, WHERE status = 'active' filters rows, while HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 keeps only groups with more than five rows. Filtering early with WHERE is also more efficient.

questions.question: How do you choose the right chart type for your data?
questions.ideal_answer: Choose based on the question and data type. Use a line chart for trends over time, a bar chart for comparing categories, a histogram or box plot for the distribution of a numeric variable, a scatter plot for the relationship between two numeric variables, and a stacked bar or, sparingly, a pie chart for parts of a whole with few categories. Heatmaps show correlation matrices or two-dimensional patterns, and maps show geographic data. Keep charts simple, label axes, start bar axes at zero and use colour purposefully.

questions.question: What are window functions in SQL? Give an example of using ROW_NUMBER or RANK.
questions.ideal_answer: Window functions compute a value across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them into one row like GROUP BY does. They use the OVER clause with optional PARTITION BY and ORDER BY. ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequential number; RANK gives tied rows the same rank and leaves gaps; DENSE_RANK has no gaps. LAG and LEAD access previous and next rows, and SUM OVER computes running totals. For example, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) and filtering where it equals 1 finds the top-paid employee in each department.

questions.question: What is the difference between correlation and causation? How would you test for causation?
questions.ideal_answer: Correlation measures how strongly two variables move together, for example with the Pearson coefficient between -1 and 1, but it does not show that one causes the other; the relationship may be driven by a confounding variable, reverse causation or coincidence. Causation is best established with a randomised controlled experiment such as an A/B test. When experiments are not possible, quasi-experimental methods such as difference-in-differences, regression with controls for confounders, instrumental variables or propensity score matching can estimate causal effects.

questions.question: How do you detect and treat outliers in a dataset?
questions.ideal_answer: Detect outliers visually with box plots, histograms and scatter plots, and statistically with the IQR rule, where values below Q1 minus 1.5 IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 IQR are flagged, or with z-scores above about 3. Then investigate whether they are data errors or genuine extreme values. Treat errors by correcting or removing them; for genuine values consider capping or winsorising, log or other transformations, using robust statistics such as the median, or analysing them separately, since outliers can be the most important insight, as in fraud.

questions.question: Daily active users dropped 15% last week. How would you investigate the cause?
questions.ideal_answer: First validate the data: check for tracking or logging bugs, pipeline failures and definition changes. Then check whether the drop is sudden or gradual and compare with seasonality, holidays and the same period last year. Segment the metric by platform, app version, country, acquisition channel, new versus returning users and user cohorts to localise the drop. Check internal events such as releases, experiments, outages and marketing changes, and external factors such as competitor launches or news. Break DAU into its funnel components, such as new user acquisition and retention, form hypotheses, validate them with data, quantify the impact and recommend actions.

questions.question: How would you perform a cohort analysis to measure customer retention?
questions.ideal_answer: Group customers into cohorts by a shared start event, usually the month of sign-up or first purchase. For each cohort, track the percentage of customers still active in each subsequent period, which produces a retention matrix with cohorts as rows and months since start as columns, often shown as a heatmap or retention curves. In SQL this uses the first activity date per user, a period index from the date difference, and counting distinct active users per cohort and period. Comparing cohorts shows whether retention is improving after product changes and where churn happens, and feeds into customer lifetime value estimates.

questions.question: How would you define success metrics and build a KPI dashboard for a new product feature?
questions.ideal_answer: Start from the feature's goal and the business objective it supports. Define a primary success metric tied to that goal, such as adoption or conversion rate, supporting metrics across the funnel such as reach, engagement and retention, and guardrail metrics such as performance, churn or support tickets to catch harm. Make each metric specific, measurable and owned, with clear definitions and targets. Ensure the events are tracked correctly, build reliable data pipelines, and design the dashboard for its audience with a few headline KPIs, trends over time, segment filters and comparisons against baseline or targets, refreshed automatically, with alerts for anomalies.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.ideal_answer: A strong answer is a concise, structured summary of about one to two minutes covering present, past and future: current role or studies, key skills and technologies, one or two relevant achievements or projects with measurable results, and why you are interested in this role and company. It stays professional and relevant to the job, and avoids reciting the whole resume or personal details.

questions.question: What are your greatest strengths and weaknesses?
questions.ideal_answer: Name two or three strengths relevant to the role and support each with a specific example from projects or work. For the weakness, choose a genuine but non-critical area, explain its impact honestly, and describe the concrete steps you are taking to improve with evidence of progress. Avoid clichés such as being a perfectionist and avoid weaknesses that are core to the job.

questions.question: Describe a time you worked in a team to achieve a goal. What was your role?
questions.ideal_answer: Use the STAR method: describe the situation and team context, the task or goal, the specific actions you personally took such as coordinating work, communicating, solving problems or supporting teammates, and the measurable result. Highlight collaboration, communication and accountability, and close with what you learned about working in teams.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a teammate. How did you handle it?
questions.ideal_answer: Use the STAR method. Describe a real disagreement professionally without blaming the other person, explain how you listened to understand their perspective, communicated openly and privately, focused on shared goals and facts, and agreed on a compromise or solution, escalating only if needed. State the positive outcome for the project and relationship and what you learned about handling conflict.

questions.question: Why do you want to work for our company?
questions.ideal_answer: Show that you researched the company: mention its products, mission, values, culture or recent achievements specifically. Connect these to your own skills, interests and career goals, and explain how you can contribute value in the role. Be genuine and specific rather than generic, and avoid focusing only on salary or perks.

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.ideal_answer: Describe realistic, ambitious goals that align with the role and the company's growth path, such as deepening technical expertise, taking ownership of larger projects, mentoring others or moving into leadership. Mention the skills you plan to develop and show commitment to growing within the organisation, without being too vague or naming an unrelated career.

questions.question: Describe the most challenging problem you have solved. How did you approach it?
questions.ideal_answer: Use the STAR method. Explain why the problem was difficult, then walk through your approach: understanding and breaking down the problem, researching, considering alternatives, testing hypotheses, seeking help when needed and implementing a solution. Quantify the result and impact and reflect on what you learned and would do differently.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed. What did you learn from it?
questions.ideal_answer: Choose a real failure, take ownership without making excuses or blaming others, and briefly explain what happened and why. Spend most of the answer on what you learned and the concrete changes you made afterwards, ideally with an example of later success that shows the lesson was applied.

questions.question: How do you handle pressure and tight deadlines?
questions.ideal_answer: Explain your practical approach: prioritising tasks by urgency and impact, breaking work into smaller milestones, planning time, communicating early with stakeholders about risks or trade-offs, staying calm and focused, and asking for help when needed. Support it with a specific STAR example where you delivered under pressure and the outcome.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you showed leadership.
questions.ideal_answer: Use the STAR method with an example from a project, club, internship or team, even without a formal title. Describe how you took initiative, set direction, delegated tasks according to strengths, motivated and supported others, made decisions and handled obstacles. Quantify the outcome and mention what you learned about leading people.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology or skill quickly.
questions.ideal_answer: Use the STAR method. Describe the situation that required the new skill and the deadline, then explain how you learned it efficiently through documentation, courses, tutorials, hands-on practice, small prototypes and asking experienced people. Describe how you applied it to deliver the result and what this shows about your adaptability and learning ability.

questions.question: Why should we hire you?
questions.ideal_answer: Summarise the specific combination of skills, experience and qualities that match the job requirements, backed by one or two evidence-based achievements. Show enthusiasm for the role and explain the value you would bring to the team and company, such as solving their problems or contributing quickly, while staying confident but not arrogant.
